did_you_know.text: Psalm 106 opens with a call to give thanks to the Lord for his goodness, emphasizing that his mercy endures forever. Thus, from the very beginning, divine mercy is presented as a central theme of the psalm.
The psalmist confesses in the plural: “We have sinned, acted wrongly, and done evil.” In doing so, he includes himself and his generation in a reflection on the sins of Israel’s ancestors.

According to the psalm, the Israelites in Egypt failed to remember the Lord’s wonders and his abundant mercy, and they rebelled at the Red Sea. Nevertheless, the Lord saved them for the sake of his name.

After witnessing the Lord’s salvation, the Israelites quickly forgot his deeds and did not wait for his counsel. The psalm presents this forgetfulness as a swift return from words of faith and praise.
The text describes how the Lord gave them what they asked for, but at the same time sent leanness into their souls. In other words, receiving their request did not necessarily bring inner blessing.

The sin of the golden calf is described as exchanging the glory of the Lord for the image of a grass-eating ox. The contrast highlights the difference between worshiping the Lord and worshiping an idol made by human hands.
Moses is portrayed as standing in the breach before the Lord to turn away his wrath and prevent destruction. According to the psalm, his intervention kept the people from being destroyed.
Phinehas rose and acted during the plague, and afterward the plague was said to have stopped. His deed was credited to him as righteousness for all generations.

At the waters of Meribah, the Israelites angered the Lord, and this brought trouble upon Moses because of them. The following verse adds that Moses rebelled against the Lord’s spirit and spoke rashly with his lips.

The psalm concludes with a prayer for salvation and for gathering the people from among the nations, so that they may give thanks to the Lord’s holy name and boast in his praise. The final verse ends with the people’s response: “Amen, Hallelujah.”
